issues.legal_issue: An initial police report and a further-investigation report are both considered in deciding whether to take cognizance, even when they reach different conclusions.
material_facts: The police initially filed a report alleging that the accused had committed offences.
After further investigation, the police filed a report recommending that proceedings against the accused be dropped.
The Magistrate had not yet decided whether to take cognizance on the reports.
issues.conclusion: Both the initial report and the further report are police reports to be considered by the Magistrate, who must decide whether to take cognizance after applying judicial mind to them.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 173(2) and 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an initial report and a further report are forwarded to the Magistrate. Under Section 190(1)(b), the Magistrate decides whether to take cognizance on a police report. Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra and Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill establish that the Magistrate may take cognizance despite a police recommendation to the contrary and must exercise judicial discretion.

predicates.criminal_case_with_initial_and_further_r: The matter is a criminal proceeding in which the police have submitted an initial report and a report after further investigation.
predicates.reports_reach_conflicting_conclusions: The initial report alleges that a person committed an offence, while the further report concludes that the person did not commit it.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding has conflicting initial and further police reports, the Magistrate considers both and decides whether to take cognizance.

issues.legal_issue: The High Court should not quash criminal proceedings before the Magistrate has considered the initial and further police reports and exercised judicial discretion on cognizance.
material_facts: An initial police report alleged that the accused had committed offences, and a later report after further investigation recommended dropping proceedings against them.
Before the Magistrate considered either report and any objections to the further report, the High Court quashed the proceedings against the accused.
The matter reached the Supreme Court in an appeal against the High Court’s quashing order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s quashing order was premature and was set aside. The further report must be placed before the Magistrate, who must consider it alongside the initial report and decide in accordance with law after considering any objections.
issues.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure preserves the High Court’s inherent power to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, but that power ordinarily should not be exercised at an interlocutory stage where the Magistrate has not considered the police reports under Sections 173(2) and 173(8) and exercised the discretion under Section 190. R. P. Kapur v. State of Punjab supports this limitation. Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra and Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill establish the Magistrate’s role in considering the reports and any complainant objections.

rule.if: appeal_against_quashing_order and initial_report_alleges_offence and further_report_recommends_dropping_proceedings and magistrate_has_not_considered_reports

predicates.appeal_against_quashing_order: The matter is an appeal from an order quashing criminal proceedings.
predicates.initial_report_alleges_offence: The initial police report alleges that the accused committed an offence.
predicates.further_report_recommends_dropping_proce: A report after further investigation recommends that proceedings against the accused be dropped.
predicates.magistrate_has_not_considered_reports: The Magistrate has not applied judicial mind to the initial and further reports or considered any objections to the further report.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a quashing order made before the Magistrate considered the reports and any objections, the quashing order is set aside and the Magistrate decides the matter after that consideration.
